results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database, which describes the mushroom body as divided into these three parts: the calyx, which receives sensory interneuron afferents; the pedunculus, a thick axon bundle extending from the calyx to the base of the lobes; and the mushroom body lobe system, consisting of a vertical branch and a medial branch with different structures at different life stages. VFB holds various data related to the mushroom body, including [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") records of neurons with some part in the mushroom body, [176](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of mushroom body") records of parts of the mushroom body, and [2](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of mushroom body") records of subclasses of the mushroom body.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response:
The types of Kenyon cells in the adult Drosophila brain include [[KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain")(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), KCab-c, [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [[Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"), as well as alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which can be further subdivided into subtypes such as core/surface/posterior, anterior-posterior/middle, and dorsal/main/gamma-s/gamma-t classes, according to VFB. VFB holds [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") records of subclasses of Kenyon cell. 

To learn more about the different types of Kenyon cells, you can explore the available data in VFB, such as the list of available images of Kenyon cell, scRNAseq data for Kenyon cell, transgene expression in Kenyon cell, downstream connectivity classes for Kenyon cell, and upstream connectivity classes for Kenyon cell.

results.response: The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") is connected to various brain regions, including the mushroom body and lateral horn. results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: The LPLC2 visual neuron type is known to be a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron with a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer. According to the information available from VFB, it detects looming (expansion) stimuli and elicits a jump escape response. The cell body of LPLC2 is located in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind. In the lobula, it has its main dendritic arbors in layers 4 and 5B, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4. Its arbors span approximately 25 lobula optic columns, overlapping with other LPLC2 cells. The LPLC2 neuron projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4. There are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe and they are cholinergic. This information is based on the work of Wu et al. (2016), Klapoetke et al. (2017), Tanaka and Clark (2022), and Davis et al. (2020), as summarized in the VFB neuron profile. VFB holds data on the LPLC2 visual neuron type, including its connections and properties.

results.title: Anatomical containment chain
results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?
results.response:
The containment hierarchy from the [antennal lobe glomerulus DA1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003932 "Open antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 in Virtual Fly Brain") up to the top-level brain structure is provided by VFB data. According to the VFB trace containment chain, one possible hierarchy is: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult olfactory antennal lobe glomerulus. Another possible hierarchy is: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum. A more detailed hierarchy is also given as: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain.

VFB holds various records related to the antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, including neurons with some part in it ([10](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") records), neurons with synaptic terminals in it (10 records), images of neurons with some part in it ([911](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") records), and transgene expression in it ([5](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") records). These records can be further explored to understand the structure and function of the antennal lobe glomerulus DA1.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, as stated by Thomas and Wyman (1984). VFB records show that the giant fiber neuron has a distinct anatomy and connectivity. 

VFB holds [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") records of images of the giant fiber neuron, specifically DNp01, which can provide insight into its anatomy. Additionally, VFB has annotated [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01, including GAL4 drivers associated with the giant fiber neuron. 

The connectome data indicates that the giant fiber neuron, DNp01, has downstream connectivity classes ([361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records) and upstream connectivity classes ([435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records), which can be explored for further understanding of its connectivity. 

For more information, you can query the VFB database for specific details on the giant fiber neuron's anatomy, connectivity, and associated driver lines. Relevant publications, such as the one by Thomas and Wyman (1984), can also be consulted for more in-depth knowledge on the giant fiber neuron's role in jump escape behavior.
